title: Quantifying Mixed-state Entanglement Via Partial Transpose And Realignment Moments
authors: Poetri Sonya Tarabunga And Tobias Haug
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2194 (2026).

Entanglement plays a crucial role in quantum information science and many-body physics, yet quantifying it in mixed quantum many-body systems has remained a notoriously difficult problem. Here, we introduce families of quantitative entanglement witnesses, constructed from partial transpose and realignment moments, which provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones as well as entanglement dimensionality. Our witnesses can be efficiently measured using SWAP tests or variants of Bell measurements, thus making them directly implementable on current hardware. Leveraging our witnesses, we present several novel results on entanglement properties of mixed states, both in quantum information and many-body physics. We develop efficient algorithms to test whether mixed states with bounded entropy have low or high entanglement, which previously was only possible for pure states. We also provide an efficient algorithm to test the Schmidt rank using only two-copy measurements, and the operator Schmidt rank using four-copy measurements. Further, our witnesses robustly certify the quantum circuit depth in the presence of noise, as well as the Schmidt rank of mixed states. Finally, we show that the entanglement phase diagram of Haar random states, quantified by the partial transpose negativity, can be fully established solely by computing our witness, a result that also applies to any state [MATH]-design. Our witnesses can also be efficiently computed for matrix product states, thus enabling the characterization of entanglement in extensive many-body systems. Finally, we make progress on the entanglement required for quantum cryptography, establishing rigorous limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices with bounded entropy. Our work opens new avenues for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems.

.
tldr: Introduces entanglement witnesses from partial transpose and realignment moments that bound entanglement monotones and dimensionality, with efficient measurement via SWAP tests.
motivation: Quantifying mixed-state entanglement is challenging; existing methods are often inefficient or limited to pure states.
method: Constructs witnesses based on partial transpose and realignment moments, measurable via SWAP tests or Bell measurements; develops algorithms for testing entanglement, Schmidt rank, and circuit depth.
result: Provides efficient algorithms for mixed states with bounded entropy, robust certification under noise, and establishes phase diagrams for Haar random states; also bounds pseudoentanglement.
conclusion: Offers practical tools for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems, with applications in many-body physics and cryptography.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state exhibiting Rényi-index-dependent entanglement scaling and introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound to diagnose such anomalous behavior from experimental data.
motivation: It is often assumed that the second Rényi entropy tracks the von Neumann entropy in scaling, but exceptions exist in constrained systems. This work generalizes such exceptions to interacting fermions and provides a practical diagnostic tool.
method: A specific number-conserving many-body state is constructed, and a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy is derived from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: The state shows a clear change in leading entanglement scaling as a function of Rényi index, and the proposed bound can detect this anomaly.
conclusion: The paper offers a protocol for identifying when Rényi entropies are not reliable proxies for von Neumann entropy, which is crucial for experimental entanglement measurements.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: A locally monitored free-fermion chain exhibits volume-law entanglement growth due to dark intervals between bunched quantum jumps.
motivation: To understand how local monitoring affects entanglement dynamics, contrasting with unitary and post-selected (no-click) limits.
method: Analyzes quantum jump trajectories of a free-fermion chain with single-site density monitoring, computing entanglement entropy and waiting-time statistics.
result: Entanglement entropy grows to a stationary volume-law state, explained by super-Poissonian waiting times with bunching and long dark intervals; increasing monitored sites drives a transition to area-law scaling via the Zeno effect.
conclusion: The presence of dark intervals is crucial for extensive entanglement growth, and the effect is suppressed when monitoring is extended to more sites.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries, enabling indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on, and demonstrates scalable performance in collective architectures.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires fast charging and the ability to halt energy transfer to prevent reverse flow. Direct control of the charger-battery interaction is experimentally demanding, motivating the need for a less invasive control method.
method: The authors propose applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit to exploit the Zeno effect, dynamically reshaping the effective Hamiltonian and switching the charger-battery coupling on and off. They analyze a minimal three-body model and extend to a collective many-body architecture, also considering an NV-center implementation.
result: The protocol remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit and preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, which scales with the number of battery units, in the many-body case.
conclusion: The modulator-assisted Zeno control offers a scalable and experimentally feasible route to regulate energy transfer in quantum batteries, with potential implementation in spin platforms.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: This paper proposes approximate compilation schemes for QAOA based on graph sparsification and decomposition, reducing circuit complexity and improving noise resilience for trapped-ion implementations.
motivation: To reduce the cost of compiling QAOA for Max-Cut on trapped-ion hardware, which suffers from noise and high circuit depth.
method: They use graph sparsification (reducing edges while preserving cut structure) and decomposition (breaking weighted graphs into unweighted ones) to design compilations with fewer MS pulses and Pauli flips, and provide theoretical guarantees.
result: They achieve asymptotic improvements in the number of MS pulses and Pauli flips, and demonstrate better approximation ratios in simulated experiments with dephasing noise.
conclusion: The techniques provide provable improvements and are expected to be useful for future quantum computing experiments across various hardware.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices with stabilizer states and Clifford operations to derive new bounds on stabilizer ranks, introduces a new magic monotone, and provides algorithms for fidelity amplification.
motivation: Quantifying non-stabilizerness (magic) is crucial for quantum computing advantages; the authors aim to improve lower bounds on stabilizer ranks and introduce new tools.
method: They study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states, and Clifford operations, prove a quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity, define the Barnes Wall norm as a new magic monotone, and present a Fidelity Amplification algorithm.
result: They show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which is linear-by-log and holds even for exponentially small fidelity, and they exhibit states achieving tight bounds for the Barnes Wall norm.
conclusion: The results provide new insights into stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, advancing the resource theory of non-stabilizerness.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamically condensed colour codes under noise bias, introduces the teraquop volume metric, and shows that repeating measurements helps under measurement-biased noise while belief matching decoding can significantly improve performance.
motivation: To enable large-scale quantum computation with dynamical stabilizer codes, it is crucial to optimize measurement schedules, especially for hardware where measurements are more error-prone than other operations.
method: The authors analyze dynamically condensed colour codes, generalize the teraquop footprint to a teraquop volume that accounts for both qubit number and measurement rounds, and compare decoding strategies (belief matching vs. minimum-weight perfect matching) across different noise bias limits.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance for measurement-biased noise models but offers little benefit for unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise; using belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one under certain noise models.
conclusion: The teraquop volume is a more informative metric than footprint alone, as performance differences are largely due to measurement rounds, and the choice of decoder critically affects code performance.

title: Floquetifying Stabiliser Codes With Distance-preserving Rewrites
authors: Benjamin Rodatz, Boldizsár Poór, And Aleks Kissinger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2202 (2026).

Stabiliser codes with large weight measurements can be challenging to implement fault-tolerantly. To overcome this, we propose a Floquetification procedure which, given a stabiliser code, synthesises a novel Floquet code that only uses single- and two-qubit operations. Moreover, this procedure preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code. The new Floquet code requires additional physical qubits. This overhead is linear in the weight of the largest measurement of the original code. Our method is based on the ZX calculus, a graphical language for representing and rewriting quantum circuits. However, a problem arises with the use of ZX in the context of rewriting error-correcting codes: ZX rewrites generally do not preserve code distance. Tackling this issue, we define the notion of distance-preserving rewrite that enables the transformation of error-correcting codes without changing their distance. These distance-preserving rewrites are used to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into quantum circuits with single- and two-qubit operations. As we only use distance-preserving rewrites, we are guaranteed that a single error in the resulting circuit creates at most a single error on the data qubits. These decompositions enable us to generalise the Floquetification procedure of Townsend-Teague et al [83] to arbitrary stabiliser codes, provably preserving the distance and number of logicals of the original code.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a Floquetification procedure that transforms arbitrary stabiliser codes into Floquet codes using only single- and two-qubit operations, while preserving code distance and logical count via distance-preserving rewrites in ZX calculus.
motivation: Large-weight stabiliser measurements are difficult to implement fault-tolerantly, so the authors aim to generate Floquet codes with only low-weight operations from any stabiliser code.
method: They define distance-preserving rewrites in ZX calculus and use them to decompose high-weight stabiliser measurements into circuits with single- and two-qubit gates, ensuring that a single error on data qubits propagates to at most one error.
result: The Floquetification preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code, with an overhead linear in the largest measurement weight, and extends previous methods to arbitrary stabiliser codes.
conclusion: This work provides a general framework for constructing low-weight Floquet codes, potentially improving fault-tolerant implementations of quantum error correction.

title: Simple Logical Quantum Computation With Concatenated Symplectic Double Codes
authors: Noah Berthusen And Elijah Durso-Sabina
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2195 (2026).

There have been significant recent advances in constructing theoretical and practical quantum error correcting codes that function well as quantum memories; however, performing fault-tolerant logical gates on these codes is less studied, and the protocols that do exist often require significant complexity. Building off the symplectic double construction, we investigate concatenated symplectic double codes, which have a rich set of logical gates implementable using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling. Combined with injected fold-transversal gates, the full Clifford group on a single codeblock is achieved through a functionally simple circuit. We perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and quantum error correction on these codes and show that they have promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates. As such, we argue that concatenated symplectic double codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code on medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

.
tldr: This paper proposes concatenated symplectic double codes that enable a simple implementation of the full Clifford group using only single-qubit gates and relabeling, with circuit-level simulations showing promising performance.
motivation: Fault-tolerant logical gates on quantum error correcting codes are often complex; the authors aim to construct codes with a rich set of implementable logical gates and good performance for medium- to large-scale quantum computers.
method: Building on the symplectic double construction, they concatenate these codes to achieve a wide set of logical gates using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling, supplemented by injected fold-transversal gates for the full Clifford group. They perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and error correction.
result: Simulations show promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates, suggesting the codes are strong candidates as computational codes.
conclusion: The authors argue that concatenated symplectic double codes offer a functionally simple approach to fault-tolerant logical Clifford gates with competitive performance, making them viable for future quantum computers.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: This paper investigates how disorder alters entanglement entropy scaling in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, revealing disorder-induced entanglement phase transitions.
motivation: Non-Hermitian systems with skin effects exhibit area-law entanglement, but the impact of disorder on this behavior is unknown, motivating this study.
method: The authors analyze the Hatano-Nelson model for free fermions with open boundaries, varying disorder strength, and compute entanglement entropy, correlation functions, and mutual information.
result: Small disorder drives the system from area-law to logarithmic entanglement scaling, while stronger disorder restores area-law through a phase transition; at criticality, entropy shows universal algebraic scaling, and conformal invariance is restored.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a partition function framework for estimating logical error curves in stabilizer codes, focusing on maximum likelihood and maximum probability decoding, with analysis of the toric code under bitflip noise.
motivation: To improve the estimation of logical error rates in quantum error correction, particularly in low-noise regimes where failure counting is inefficient.
method: They define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to decoding success probabilities, map the toric code bitflip noise to the Random Bond Ising Model, and demonstrate more sample-efficient estimation than direct failure counting.
result: The partition function approach is more sample-efficient, especially at low noise, and they discuss effects of degeneracy among maximum probability errors and ensembling.
conclusion: The framework provides a powerful tool for evaluating decoding performance in stabilizer codes, with potential applications to other codes and noise models.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for robust topological quantum state transfer using long-range interactions in Rydberg atom chains, demonstrating improved fidelity and robustness compared to nearest-neighbor models.
motivation: To achieve fast, robust, and high-fidelity quantum state transfer in chains with long-range couplings, motivated by Rydberg platforms, where topological protection can be enhanced.
method: Use extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) and Rice-Mele models with long-range couplings to support topologically protected edge states; implement both time-independent coherent edge state dynamics and time-dependent adiabatic modulation protocols.
result: Long-range couplings increase relevant energy gaps, significantly improving transfer efficiency and robustness against disorder compared to nearest-neighbor models.
conclusion: Long-range interacting platforms like Rydberg arrays are promising for reliable quantum state transfer due to topological protection and enhanced energy gaps.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: This paper presents an optimized linear optics scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states with fewer photons and higher success rates compared to fusion-based approaches, using the linear quantum graph picture.
motivation: Graph states are essential for quantum information processing, but current photonic generation methods via fusion gates are inefficient in terms of photon number and success rates, especially for complex states like caterpillar graph states.
method: The scheme uses only single-photon sources, linear optical elements, and heralded measurements to directly generate caterpillar graph states, based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) framework.
result: For caterpillar graph states of a given length, the method requires fewer photons and achieves a success rate that is significantly higher than fusion-based approaches.
conclusion: The study demonstrates that the LQG picture offers a powerful and flexible route for efficiently generating complex photonic graph states, thereby advancing quantum information processing.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: A Bayesian framework for multiparameter quantum estimation is presented, showing that measurement incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss.
motivation: To understand the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation and its effect on attainable precision.
method: Derive upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement and evaluate the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound.
result: Prove that incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealized scenario with individually optimal measurements.
conclusion: The results provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that with a suitable catalyst state, the T-depth of any single-qubit z-rotation can be reduced to a constant, enabling constant-T-depth approximations of multi-qubit gates.
motivation: Reducing T-depth is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing since T gates are expensive. The paper explores catalytic approaches to achieve constant T-depth for common unitaries.
method: The authors construct a catalyst state and show that for any single-qubit z-rotation, there exists a Clifford+T circuit with constant T-depth that approximates it using the catalyst. They prove the required catalyst size scales polynomially with the target precision and that the catalyst can be prepared in polynomial time.
result: Any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated with constant T-depth using a polynomial-sized catalyst. This also implies that multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform can be approximated with constant T-depth circuits.
conclusion: The result improves the efficiency of quantum circuits by reducing T-depth without increasing resource overhead beyond polynomial, suggesting practical benefits for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: This paper compares two leading surface code lattice surgery compilation schemes for Hamiltonian simulation, showing that the optimal approach depends on the simulation algorithm (Trotter-Suzuki vs. quantum signal processing).
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing resource estimates often assume a particular surface code compilation method, but it is unclear if one scheme is universally better. This work investigates whether direct Clifford+T compilation or serialized compilation (eliminating Clifford gates) yields lower resource costs for Hamiltonian simulation.
method: The authors analyze resource costs (e.g., T-count, spacetime volume) for simulating transverse-field Ising, Kitaev honeycomb, and a time-dependent magnetic field model, using both compilation schemes and two simulation algorithms (Trotter-Suzuki and quantum signal processing).
result: Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation, while quantum signal processing may favor the serialized approach. The optimal scheme depends on circuit-level properties like logical qubit count, T fraction, and average circuit density.
conclusion: Surface code quantum processors should adopt adaptive compilation strategies that predict the best scheme based on high-level circuit characteristics, rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all method.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error-correction performance and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for reliable quantum computing and communication, but existing codes often have high overhead or limited structure; the authors aim to design efficient codes with good performance.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, derive rate expressions, and propose an encoding scheme. They evaluate performance using a quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum decoder against depolarizing and Markovian noise.
result: The proposed codes achieve nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance compared to layered binary sum-product decoding, and outperform prior work under random and burst errors.
conclusion: The scalable code constructions and enhanced decoding demonstrate practical potential for quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: The paper introduces atommovr, an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in atomic arrays, and uses it to study time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species rearrangement, including a novel algorithm InsideOut.
motivation: Atom rearrangement is fundamental for neutral-atom quantum processors, and there is a lack of open-source tools for benchmarking algorithms, especially under noise.
method: The authors developed an open-source simulation framework and used it to analyze three settings: time-optimal noiseless, noisy with realistic error models, and noiseless dual-species. They also proposed the dual-species algorithm InsideOut.
result: They extracted lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identified advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrated that InsideOut can avoid blocked configurations with near-unity success rate.
conclusion: The framework aims to serve as a community tool for studying rearrangement, lower the barrier for new groups, and stimulate progress in algorithms to minimize atom loss.

title: Reducing Spatial And Temporal Dimensionality In The Multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett Model
authors: Hongfei Zhan, Ernest W.Z. Pan, And Zhenning Cai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2201 (2026).

Focusing on the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, several techniques are adopted in this paper to reduce the spatial and temporal dimensionality, combined into an efficient algorithm. From a spatial perspective, an equivalent formulation of the Dyson series is presented. With the aid of a low-rank approximation, the spatial dimensionality of open quantum system simulations is halved. From a temporal perspective, the frozen Gaussian approximation is used to approximate both the evolution operator and the interaction operator in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model. This reduces the high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the truncation level of the Dyson series. Through these techniques, we design an efficient algorithm whose validity is verified through several numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double slit simulation.

.
tldr: This paper presents an efficient algorithm for simulating the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model by reducing both spatial and temporal dimensionality using low-rank approximations and frozen Gaussian approximations.
motivation: Simulating open quantum systems in multiple dimensions is computationally prohibitive; the authors aim to develop a method that scales better with dimensionality.
method: They combine an equivalent Dyson series formulation with low-rank approximation to halve spatial dimensions, and use frozen Gaussian approximations to reduce high-dimensional integrals to low-dimensional ones independent of the Dyson truncation level.
result: The algorithm is validated through numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double slit simulation, demonstrating accuracy and efficiency.
conclusion: The proposed techniques provide a practical approach to simulate multidimensional open quantum systems, significantly reducing computational cost while preserving accuracy.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide theory-dependent methods for detecting nonclassicality that complement theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs to certify nonclassicality and demonstrate the framework with explicit examples.
result: They introduce efficient SDP-based certificates and witnesses that can be applied to individual states and measurements, offering practical detection tools.
conclusion: The framework advances the characterization of nonclassicality and complements existing inequalities, with potential applications in quantum information.

title: Non-secular Polariton Leakage And Dark-state Protection In Hybrid Plasmonic Cavities
authors: Marco Vallone
abstract: A major issue in exploiting plasmonic cavities as key components in nanotechnology is the effect of radiative and absorption losses on their electrodynamic behavior. Treating them as open systems, we derive a time-local, completely positive master equation that retains non-secular interference between decay pathways and reduces to the standard secular description when the environment resolves polariton splitting. When it does not, the theory predicts order-one deviations from secular leakage dynamics, including bath-induced coherences and formation of a comparatively long-lived dark polaritonic component, and provides a simple design criterion based on the ratio of polariton splitting to reservoir linewidth. A time-resolved leakage measurement, such as transmission, reflectivity, or photoluminescence, can be used to observe these effects.
tldr: The paper derives a non-secular master equation for hybrid plasmonic cavities, predicting bath-induced coherences and long-lived dark polaritonic states.
motivation: To accurately describe leakage dynamics in lossy plasmonic cavities where the standard secular approximation may fail.
method: Derives a time-local, completely positive master equation that retains non-secular interference terms and reduces to secular when environment resolves polariton splitting.
result: Predicts order-one deviations from secular leakage, including bath-induced coherences and long-lived dark polaritonic component, with a design criterion based on polariton splitting to reservoir linewidth ratio.
conclusion: Time-resolved measurements can observe these effects, providing insights for designing low-loss plasmonic cavities.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut Via Qudit Swap Operators
authors: Igor Klep, Tea Štrekelj, And Jurij Volčič
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2203 (2026).

Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max [MATH]-Cut ([MATH]-QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with [MATH] vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on [MATH]. The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree [MATH]. This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the [MATH]-QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined [MATH]-QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For general [MATH], low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

.
tldr: This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of Quantum Max Cut, deriving an SDP hierarchy and exact solutions for certain graphs using representation theory.
motivation: To understand the algebraic and computational complexity of the Quantum Max d-Cut problem, a generalization of Quantum Max Cut to qudits, and to develop efficient optimization methods.
method: The authors identify the algebra generated by swap operators as a quotient of a free algebra, use noncommutative polynomial optimization to build an SDP hierarchy, and apply representation theory of symmetric groups for specific graph classes.
result: They derive exact solutions for complete bipartite graphs and show that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes isotypic components, providing low-degree relations for separation.

title: A Brief History Of Quantum Vs Classical Computational Advantage
authors: Ryan Larose
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2198 (2026).

In this review article we summarize all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage to date. Our review highlights challenges, loopholes, and refutations appearing in subsequent work to provide a complete picture of the current statuses of these experiments. In addition, we also discuss theoretical computational advantage in example problems such as approximate optimization and recommendation systems. Finally, we review recent experiments in quantum error correction --- the biggest frontier to reach experimental quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm.

.
tldr: A review of experiments and theoretical results on quantum computational advantage, including challenges, loopholes, and recent quantum error correction efforts.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the current status of quantum computational advantage experiments and theoretical discussions.
method: Summarizes all claimed experiments, discusses challenges and refutations, and reviews theoretical examples and quantum error correction experiments.
result: Presents a complete picture of the statuses of these experiments and discusses the path toward quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm via error correction.
conclusion: Quantum computational advantage has been demonstrated in specific settings, but challenges remain; quantum error correction is the frontier for achieving advantage in Shor's algorithm.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: This paper proves an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum circuits and constant-depth classical circuits with bounded fan-in and limited randomness for a sampling task.
motivation: To answer a question posed by Bravyi et al. about whether a separation between shallow quantum and classical circuits exists for input-independent sampling tasks.
method: The authors introduce a specific distribution and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family that samples close to it, while proving lower bounds on the depth of any bounded fan-in classical circuit that approximates it given a bounded number of random input bits.
result: They show unconditionally that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that cannot be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error, and extend this to a separation with advice and unbounded randomness.
conclusion: This demonstrates an unconditional quantum advantage in sampling with shallow circuits, but it is a computational complexity result rather than directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Non-Gaussian Noise Magnetometry Using Local Spin Qubits
authors: Jonathan B. Curtis, Amir Yacoby, And Eugene Demler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2197 (2026).

Atomic scale qubits, as may be realized in nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, offer the opportunity to study magnetic field noise with nanometer scale spatial resolution. Using these spin qubits, one can learn a great deal about the magnetic-field noise correlations, and correspondingly the collective-mode spectra, in quantum materials and devices. However, to date these tools have been essentially restricted to studying Gaussian noise processes – equivalent to linear-response. In this work we will show how to extend these techniques beyond the Gaussian regime and show how to unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved way. We unveil two protocols for doing this; the first uses a single spin-qubit and different dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise. The second protocol uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to study spatially non-local cumulants in the magnetic noise. We then demonstrate the utility of these protocols by considering a model of a bath of non-interacting two-level systems, as well as a model involving spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising phase transition. In both cases, we highlight how this technique can be used to measure in a real many-body system how fluctuation dynamics converge towards the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size. We then conclude by discussing some promising applications and extensions of this method.

.
tldr: This paper introduces protocols to measure non-Gaussian magnetic noise using spin qubits, enabling higher-order cumulant detection and local noise characterization in many-body systems.
motivation: Standard spin-qubit magnetometry is limited to Gaussian noise (linear response). The authors aim to extend these techniques to non-Gaussian noise to study anharmonic, non-Markovian, and spatially non-local correlations.
method: They propose two protocols: one using a single spin qubit with tailored dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Gaussian and non-Markovian spin-echo noise spectra, and another using two spin qubits to characterize spatial correlations beyond Gaussian approximation.

title: Floquet Approach To Graphene: Spectral Metamorphosis, Quantum Poincare Recurrences, And Lissajous Curves
authors: M Inglot, L Chotorlishvili, A Dyrdał, V K Dugaev, J Barnaś And A Sinner
abstract: The Floquet formalism, developed for systems driven periodically in time, is applied to graphene, including the Rashba spin–orbit and Zeeman terms. Employing the high-frequency approximation, we studied Floquet-induced reconstruction of the Dirac spectrum, Poincaré recurrences, and the associated single-particle recurrences, as well as Lissajous curves. We observed single-particle Floquet subharmonic resonances, closed stroboscopic trajectories, and a Floquet-induced topological Lifshitz-like reconstruction of the low-energy spectrum, including anisotropic Dirac-cone deformation and Dirac-cone merging. Our main focus is on periodic time-driving via femtosecond half-cycle laser pulses. We also analyze the quantum metric—the distance between the initial and evolved wave functions—in terms of the participation rates of different bands and commensurate (non-commensurate) properties of the Floquet eigenvalues. In the weak-driving regime, we observe open curves, indicating non-periodic dynamics in the system. Within the considered single-particle Floquet framework, we identify conditions under which the stroboscopic dynamics is dominated by commensurate Floquet phases, leading to quantum Poincaré recurrences, closed Lissajous trajectories, and subharmonic spin oscillations. These effects are interpreted as Floquet time-crystal-like precursors in the sense of single-particle subharmonic dynamics. Within the presented single-particle Floquet framework, Poincaré recurrences and Lissajous resonances provide criteria for closed stroboscopic trajectories and subharmonic Floquet resonances.
tldr: This paper applies Floquet theory to graphene with spin-orbit and Zeeman couplings to study spectral reconstruction, Poincaré recurrences, and Lissajous curves under periodic driving.
motivation: Investigate the effects of periodic laser pulses on graphene's electronic properties, focusing on single-particle Floquet dynamics and potential topological changes.
method: Employ high-frequency Floquet approximation to derive effective Hamiltonians and analyze stroboscopic evolution, participation rates, quantum metric, and subharmonic resonances.
result: Observed Floquet-induced Dirac cone deformation and merging, closed stroboscopic trajectories, and subharmonic spin oscillations, interpreted as time-crystal-like precursors.
conclusion: The study provides criteria for closed trajectories and subharmonic resonances in driven graphene, but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
authors: I.J. David, I. Sinayskiy, And F. Petruccione
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2204 (2026).

When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

.
tldr: This paper introduces randomized algorithms (including the QDRIFT channel) for simulating Markovian open quantum systems, achieving better gate complexity than deterministic Trotter-Suzuki methods.
motivation: Accurate and efficient quantum simulation of open quantum systems is essential but traditionally relies on deterministic Trotter-Suzuki or probabilistic methods that may sacrifice physicality or scalability.
method: Novel non-probabilistic randomized Trotter-Suzuki formulas and a QDRIFT channel are developed, with error bounds and step count limits derived via a new proof technique avoiding the mixing lemma, and implemented using Classical Sampling.
result: The randomized algorithms demonstrate gate complexity advantages over deterministic Trotter-Suzuki product formulas while preserving the physicality of evolution.
conclusion: Randomization techniques from Hamiltonian simulation are systematically extended to Markovian open quantum systems, offering faster and more accurate quantum simulations.

title: Symmetry-enriched Topological Order In Tensor Networks: Defects, Gauging And Anyon Condensation
authors: Dominic J. Williamson, Nick Bultinck, And Frank Verstraete
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2199 (2026).

We study symmetry-enriched topological order in two-dimensional tensor network states by using graded matrix product operator algebras to represent symmetry-induced domain walls. A close connection to the theory of graded unitary fusion categories is established. Tensor network representations of the topological defect superselection sectors are constructed for all domain walls. The emergent symmetry-enriched topological order is extracted from these representations, including the symmetry action on the underlying anyons. Dual phase transitions, induced by gauging a global symmetry, and condensation of a bosonic subtheory, are analyzed and the relationship between topological orders on either side of the transition is derived. Several examples are worked through explicitly.

.
tldr: This paper studies symmetry-enriched topological order in two-dimensional tensor networks using graded matrix product operator algebras to represent symmetry-induced domain walls, connecting to graded unitary fusion categories.
motivation: To understand the structure of symmetry-enriched topological phases and their defects, and to derive dualities via gauging and condensation.
method: The authors use graded matrix product operator algebras to represent domain walls, construct tensor network representations of topological defect superselection sectors, and analyze emergent symmetry-enriched topological order.
result: They extract the symmetry action on anyons and derive relationships between topological orders across phase transitions induced by gauging and anyon condensation, with explicit examples.
conclusion: Provides a rigorous tensor network framework for describing and analyzing symmetry-enriched topological order, advancing the mathematical understanding of such phases.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: Through dequantization and complexity analysis, the paper shows that simulating short-time classical linear dynamics with local interactions cannot achieve exponential quantum advantage, while long-time dynamics is as hard as polynomial-space quantum computation.
motivation: To determine whether quantum computers can exponentially speed up simulation of classical systems with local interactions, as opposed to previous work with long-range interactions.
method: The authors analyze the problem using complexity theory: they dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics and relate the problems to probabilistic and quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics is dequantizable (no exponential advantage), while long-time dynamics is shown to be as hard as polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting possible advantages under polynomial-space constraints.
conclusion: The work characterizes the computational complexity boundary for simulating local classical dynamics on quantum computers, clarifying when quantum advantage might emerge.

title: Universally Diverging Grüneisen Ratio Of Holographic Quantum Criticality
authors: Jun-Kun Zhao, Enze Lv, Wei Li And Li Li
abstract: Quantum criticality is a hallmark of strongly correlated electron systems, as seen in heavy-fermion materials and high-temperature superconductors. Holographic duality provides a powerful framework to investigate these systems by translating them into weakly coupled classical gravity living in one higher dimension. Here, we exploit this approach to study a field-induced quantum critical point with dynamical exponent in Einstein–Maxwell–Chern–Simons theory. Our analysis of its thermodynamic properties reveals a new universality class. Notably, we identify a diverging Grüneisen ratio with universal scaling , a behavior that closely mirrors recent experiments on the heavy-fermion material CeRh Ge . These findings advance our understanding of metallic quantum criticality and highlight the potential of holographic duality as a powerful tool for studying correlated quantum matter as well as its magnetocaloric applications.
tldr: This paper applies holographic duality to study a field-induced quantum critical point, uncovering a universally diverging Grüneisen ratio that matches heavy-fermion experiments.
motivation: To understand quantum criticality in strongly correlated electron systems using holographic methods.
method: They analyze the Einstein-Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory holographically and compute thermodynamic properties to examine the Grüneisen ratio.
result: They find a diverging Grüneisen ratio with universal scaling, indicating a new universality class, and it mirrors experimental observations in CeRhGe.
conclusion: The findings advance understanding of metallic quantum criticality and show holography's potential for studying correlated quantum matter and magnetocaloric applications.
